title: Two standards
hook: two banners: riches, honor, pride; and poverty, humiliation, humility

segments.voice: Yesterday, the call of the king: a good king shares the hard part, and how much more Christ. Your line was I want to follow. Where did you see someone walk into the work first? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-five.

On a crowded field, a banner tells you where your side is standing. Lose sight of it and you can end up fighting in the wrong company without ever deciding to. Ignatius takes that picture, from the world he knew as a soldier, and plants two banners in front of the person praying. Two flags, two leaders, two plans. The surprise is not that one is good and one is bad. Everyone expects that. The surprise is how small the first step is under each one. Today: two standards.
screen: `A BANNER SHOWS WHERE YOUR SIDE IS.` → `TWO FLAGS, TWO LEADERS.` → `HOW SMALL THE FIRST STEP IS.`

segments.voice: A standard is a banner, the flag a company gathers under. Ignatius sets up two of them on two fields. On one, near Babylon, the enemy of our human nature sits on a throne of fire and smoke, frightening to look at, and sends his helpers out into every town with a plan in three steps. First, riches. Then, once a person has things, the honor that comes with them: being seen, being admired. Then, from honor, pride. And from pride, Ignatius says, the other vices follow. On the other field, near Jerusalem, Christ stands in a lowly place, beautiful and gracious, and sends his friends out with three steps of his own. First, poverty: poverty of spirit, and actual poverty if God chooses it for someone. Then a willingness to bear insult and being overlooked. From those comes humility, and from humility, the other virtues. Notice how quiet the first step is on each side. Nobody leaps into pride. It starts with wanting a little more, and then wanting to be noticed for having it. And Christ's first step is just as small: holding things lightly, the indifference from three days ago. Jesus says it plainly in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "No man can serve two masters." The meditation ends with three conversations, asking Our Lady, then the Son, then the Father for the grace to be received under Christ's standard. Ignatius closes each with a prayer the Church already knows: a Hail Mary, the Soul of Christ, an Our Father. In daily life, the first banner rarely looks evil. It can look like a nicer car, a bigger title, winning the argument in the group chat.
screen: `A STANDARD IS A BANNER.` · `RICHES, THEN HONOR, THEN PRIDE.` · `POVERTY, THEN INSULT, THEN HUMILITY.` · `THE FIRST STEP IS SMALL.` · then, large: `NO MAN CAN SERVE TWO MASTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice which banner pulls you. Settle, and breathe. Walk back through the last day or two. Where did you feel the tug of a first step: wanting a little more, wanting to be seen, needing to be right? Don't scold yourself. Just notice it, the way you'd notice wind on your face. Then look for one moment that leaned the other way: letting someone else take the credit, going without, keeping quiet when you could have scored a point. If you pray, you can ask, as the Exercises do, for the grace to be received under Christ's standard. The bell holds the time.
Two standards. Two banners on two fields, each with a plan in three small steps: riches, honor, pride; or poverty, insult, humility. Today's word.
Your line: under his standard. Today, when you catch yourself reaching for a little more praise, a little more stuff, say the line and let one chance go by. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: In the second week of an Ignatian retreat, people pray the meditation on the two standards and end it with a triple colloquy to Mary, to Christ and to the Father, closing with the Hail Mary, the Anima Christi and the Our Father.

fork.setup: in Ignatius's meditation, you're the enemy planning how to pull someone away from God. where do you start?
options: with riches: a little more than they need.
fork.reveal: Ignatius has the enemy start with riches, then honor, then pride. the first step looks harmless, and that's the point.

original.note: Spanish, the language Ignatius wrote in: two banners, two flags.

trapdoor: what you thought: a standard is a rule, or a level of quality.
what it means: a banner on a field. Ignatius sets two before the person praying, Christ's and the enemy's.
what a scholar hears: the two plans mirror each other step for step: riches against poverty, honor against insult, pride against humility.

sources.quoted: No man can serve two masters.

sources.ref: Spiritual Exercises, meditation on two standards (no. 136–147)

notes: The meditation is paraphrased throughout (Babylon and Jerusalem fields, throne of fire and smoke, 'lowly place, beautiful and gracious', the three steps on each side, the triple colloquy with Hail Mary, Anima Christi and Our Father). Confirm details against the text.
'From pride, the other vices follow' and 'from humility, the other virtues' paraphrase no. 142 and no. 146; confirm.
Ignatius calls the leader of the first standard Lucifer and 'the mortal enemy of our human nature'; the script uses the second phrase only.
Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 6:24 to confirm. Original: Spanish 'dos banderas'; confirm.
Editor: the repeated 'On an ordinary Tuesday' closer replaced and softened ('can look like').
